# Explore drug screen datasets

## Load packages

```{r}
# Load packages for data wrangling and visualisation 
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
```

```{r}
# Load drug screen data (plate1, plate_meta and compound_dict)
load("data/drugscreen.Rda")

# Check whether datasets contain any missing values 
anyNA(plate1)
anyNA(plate_meta)
anyNA(compound_dict)

# plate1 and plate_meta don't have any NA values 
# Inspect missing values and column summaries in compound_dict
summary(compound_dict)
```

Inspection of the supplied data indicated that the luminescence plate (`plate1`) and compound plate map (`plate_meta`) had no missing values. The compound dictionary contained a missing HGNC symbol for compound 6618.

# Question 1: Using the geom_tile() function, visualise the luminescence across the plate. Are there appear to be any spatial patterns in this data?

## Prepare plate1 dataset for plotting

plate1 contains luminescence (RLU) values, and will therefore be used to answer Q1. It is arranged as rows and columns. To plot one tile per well using ggplot2, the plate must be in long format containing well coordinages and luminescence (in RLU)

```{r}
# Convert plate1 from wide to long format (where each row represents 1 well)

plate1_long <- plate1 |> 
  pivot_longer(
    # collapse all columns into 1 column except plate_row 
    cols = -plate_row, 
    # all columns collapsed into 1 column named "plate_col"
    names_to = "plate_col", 
    # all RLU values in column named "luminescence"
    values_to = "luminescence"
  )

# Check that pivot_longer() worked 
print(head(plate1_long))

# Convert plate_row and plate_col values from character to numeric 
# using parse_number() for 'tidier' data

plate1_long <- plate1_long |> 
  mutate(
    # keep numbers after "row"
    plate_row = parse_number(plate_row),
    # keep numbers after "col"
    plate_col = parse_number(plate_col))

# Check that reformatitng worked in the first few rows 
head(plate1_long)
```

## Visualise luminescence as heatmap

Loading esquisse

```{r}
# Install and load esquisse

remotes::install_github("dreamRs/esquisse")

library(esquisse)

esquisse::esquisser(plate1_long)
```

Copy/paste code from esquisse below:

```{r}
ggplot(plate1_long) +
  
  aes(x = plate_col, y = plate_row, fill = luminescence) +
  geom_tile(
    colour = "grey50", 
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", direction = 1) +
  # label every 2nd column number at the top to avoid over-crowding x-acis
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 48, by = 2), expand = c(0, 0), position = "top") +
  # reverse y-axis so plate row 1 appears at the top
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = seq(1, 32, by = 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_equal() +
  # add title, axes titles and legend
  labs(
    x = "Column",
    y = "Row",
    title = "Luminescence across 1536-well plate after 24h MPP exposure",
    fill = "Luminescence (RLU)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12L,
                              face = "bold",
                              hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10L),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10L)
  )
```

## Answer

There did not appear to be a clear spatial pattern in the heatmap. Wells with higher and lower RLU values were distributed across the 1536-well plate, without any obvious directional gradients.

# Question 2: Which compounds are statistically significantly associated with increased neuronal viability after MPP exposure? Ensure that you check your assumptions.

## Match luminescence data with compound plate map

The plate metadata must be reshaped using the same well coordinates as the luminescence data. Joining by both row and column ensures that each RLU measurement is matched to the correct compound and condition.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Convert compound plate map into one row per well 
cmpd_long <- plate_meta |> 
  pivot_longer(
    # collapse all columns into 1 column except plate_row 
    cols = -plate_row, 
    # all columns collapsed into 1 column named "plate_col"
    names_to = "plate_col", 
    # Compound and condition label for each well 
    values_to = "cmpd"
  )

# Check that pivot_longer() worked
View(cmpd_long)

# Use same numeric row/column format as plate1_long
cmpd_long <- cmpd_long |> 
  mutate(
    # keep numbers after "row"
    plate_row = parse_number(plate_row),
    # keep numbers after "col"
    plate_col = parse_number(plate_col))

# Join luminescence measurements to compound labels using well coordinates
combined_data <- plate1_long |> 
  left_join(cmpd_long, 
            by = c("plate_row", "plate_col"))

# Check that left_join() worked
View(cmpd_long)
```

## Separate compound ID and condition (ctrl/test)

The labels contain the compound number and whether a well belongs to the test (test) or control (ctrl) condition. Separating these components makes it possible to compare conditions within each compound.

```{r}
# Replace cmpd column with two new columns for the cmpd number and 
# condition (ctrl/test)
combined_data <- combined_data |> 
  separate(
    cmpd,
    into = c("prefix", "cmpd", "cond"),
    sep = "_"
  ) |> 
  # remove prefix
  select(-prefix)

# Check two new columns contain the cmpd number and the condition type
View(combined_data)

# Check whether each compound has 4 wells for each condition
combined_data  |> 
  count(cmpd, cond) |> 
  filter(n != 4)
```

## Summarise luminescence for each compound and condition

For each compound, the mean and standard deviation describe the RLU measurements within the test and control groups. The difference and percentage change quantify the direction and magnitude of test vs. control response, with higher luminescence interpreted as consistent with greater cell survival/growth.

```{r}
summary_data <- combined_data |> 
  group_by(cmpd, cond) |> 
  summarise(
    mean_lum = mean(luminescence), # mean RLU for each compound and condition
    sd_lum = sd(luminescence), # variation between replicate wells 
    n = n(), # number of replicate wells 
    .groups = "drop"
    )
# Check summary dataset created includes mean_lum and sd_lum columns
View(summary_data)

# Put control and test means side-by-side for easier comparison
comparison_data <- summary_data |> 
  select(cmpd, cond, mean_lum) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = cond,
    values_from = mean_lum
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    difference = test - ctrl, # positive = higher RLU in test wells 
    percent_change = 100 * (test - ctrl) / ctrl
  )

View(comparison_data)
```

## Assumption 1: Independence of observations

The t-test assumes that observations within and between the compared groups are independent. The four wells per condition are technical replicates. Although they are separate wells, they may share plate-lvel

## Assumption 2: Outcome is approximately normally distributed within each group

Normality can be explored using Q-Q plots of residuals centred within each compound-condition group, followed by Shapiro-Wilk tests for individual groups. Centring removes differences in group means before inspeciting the pooled residual distributions.

```{r}
# Install and load "rstatix" package

install.packages("rstatix")
library(rstatix)
```

Generate Q-Q plots to accept/reject normality

```{r}
# Subtract each compound-condition mean to obtain within-group residuals
residual_data <- combined_data |>
  group_by(cmpd, cond) |>
  mutate(
    residual = luminescence - mean(luminescence)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Check that residual column was added  
View(residual_data)

# Compare residuals with a theoretical normal distribution across separate 
# panels to allow control/test residuals to be viewed independently

ggplot(residual_data, aes(sample = residual)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~cond) +
  labs(
    title = "Q-Q plots of within-group residuals",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Residual luminescence (RLU)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Run Shapiro-Wilk test within each compound-condition group 
shapiro_results <- combined_data |>
  group_by(cmpd, cond) |>
  summarise(
    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(luminescence)$p.value,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Count groups with p < 0.05; summarise screening
shapiro_results |>
  summarise(
    total_tests = n(),
    p_below_05 = sum(shapiro_p < 0.05),
    percentage = mean(shapiro_p < 0.05) * 100
  )
```

The Q-Q plots showed that residuals were broadly consistent with normality, with some deviations in the tails. Of 384 compound-condition groups, 26 (6.8%) had Shapiro-Wilk p-values below 0.05. This is not strong evidence of widespread departures from normality, although each test uses only four observations and therefore has limited power. The pooled Q-Q plots can also conceal differences between individual groups. Together, these results provide no strong evidence against normality within groups, so the normality assumption was considered reasonable and a parametric t-test was appropriate

## Assumption 3: Equal variance

The conventional Student's t-test assumes equal population variances. To investigate this, the sample variances of test and control wells were compared for each compound. The variance ratio is calculated by dividing the larger sample variance by the smaller, so a value close to 1 indicates similar observed variation.

```{r}
# Compare sample variances of control and test wells for each compound
variance_check <- summary_data |>
  select(cmpd, cond, sd_lum) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = cond,
    values_from = sd_lum
  ) |>
  mutate(
    var_ctrl = ctrl^2, # Variance = sd^2
    var_test = test^2,
    variance_ratio = pmax(var_ctrl, var_test) /
      pmin(var_ctrl, var_test) # larger variance divided by smaller 
  )

View(variance_check)

# Summarise distribution of variance rations across all compounds
summary(variance_check$variance_ratio)
```

The variance ratios ranged from 1.005 to 91.467, with a median of 2.348. Thus, some compounds had similar test and control sample variances while others differed substantially. With only four wells per condition, the estimated variances are themselves uncertain, so the equal variance assumption could not be confidently supported across all compounds.

## Welch t-test

Following assessment of the statistical assumptions, a one-sided Welch's t-test has been selected to compare luminescence between test and control conditions for each of the 192 compounds.

```{r}

# Perform a Welch's t-test for each compound

welch_results <- combined_data |>
  # Group data by compound to perform a seperate t-test for each
  group_by(cmpd) |>
  t_test(
    luminescence ~ cond, # Compare luminescence between ctrl/group conditions
    var.equal = FALSE, # Welch's t-test allows for unequal variances
    alternative = "less", # Test whether ctrl RLUs < test RLUs
    p.adjust.method = "none" # Retain unadjusted p-values 
    # Remove grouping before multiple testing correction
  ) |> ungroup() |> 
  # Apply BH correction across all compounds to control for 
  # the false discovery rate from multiple testing 
  adjust_pvalue(method = "BH")
```

```{r}

# Identify compound with statistically significant differences in luminescence 
# following multiple-testing correction

significant_compounds <- welch_results |>
  # Filter for compounds with BH-adjusted p-values < 0.05
  filter(p.adj < 0.05) |>
  # Arrange compounds in ascending order of adjusted p-value
  arrange(p.adj)
```

```{r}
hits_data <- combined_data |>
  filter(cmpd %in% significant_compounds$cmpd) |> 
  mutate(cmpd = as.factor(cmpd))

hits_summary <- hits_data |>
  group_by(cmpd, cond) |>
  summarise(
    mean_lum = mean(luminescence),
    sd_lum = sd(luminescence),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}

ggplot(hits_data,
       aes(x = factor(cmpd),
           y = luminescence,
           colour = cond,       # Keeps summary stats color-coded
           group = cond)) +
  
  # Individual replicate measurements
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitterdodge(
      jitter.width = 0.12,
      dodge.width = 0.5
    ),
    alpha = 0.7,                # Made slightly more transparent to sit in background
    size = 1,                 # Made smaller as requested
    colour = "black"           # Forces replicates to be grey (change to "black" if preferred)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Luminescence (RLU)",            # Change the label text
    breaks = seq((min(hits_data$luminescence)-65), max(hits_data$luminescence) + 20, by = 50), 
    limits = c(400, 750)) +
  
  # Mean luminescence
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
    size = 2
  ) +
  
  # Standard deviation
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_sdl,
    fun.args = list(mult = 1),
    geom = "errorbar",
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
    width = 0.15,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Neuronal viability following MPP exposure",
    subtitle = "Luminescence of significant compounds (mean ± SD; n = 4)",
    x = "Compound ID",
    colour = "Condition"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Centre title and subtitle
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      face = "bold",
      size = 18,
      margin = margin(b = 8)
    ),
    
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 12,
      colour = "grey40",
      margin = margin(b = 15)
    ),
    
    # Increase distance between axis titles and axes
    axis.title.x = element_text(
      margin = margin(t = 15),
      size = 12
    ),
    
    axis.title.y = element_text(
      margin = margin(r = 15),
      size = 12
    ),
    
    # Improve axis tick labels
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
    
    # Reduce visual clutter
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Move legend to bottom
    legend.position = "bottom",
    
    # Add padding around the entire graph
    plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 15, 20)
  )
```

# Question 3: What are the mechanisms of action and targets of the compounds you identify in Q2?

```{r}
# Join compound_dict to comparison_data to obtain information about
# each compound's biological target and action

# Load stringr package for string manipulation
library(stringr)

# Retain all rows from comparison_data and match cmpd info
comparison_data <- comparison_data |>
  left_join(
    compound_dict |>
      # Remove "cmpd_" prefix from compound IDs to match 
      # the format of the cmpd column in comparison_data 
      mutate(cmpd = str_remove(id, "^cmpd_")) |>
      # Remove original ID column as no longer needed
      select(-id),
    # Match the two datasets using compound identifier
    by = "cmpd"
  )

# Identify the biological targets and mechanism of actions of previously identified significant compounds from Q2
significant_hits <- comparison_data |>
  # Retain only compounds identified as significant in Q2
  filter(cmpd %in% significant_compounds$cmpd) |>
  # Display compound ID, target, action and HGNC symbol
  select(
    `Compound ID` = cmpd, 
    Action = action,
    `Target Gene ID` = target_enzyme, 
    `Target HGNC` = hgnc_symbol) 
```

All four of the compounds that are statistically significantly associated with increased neuronal viability following MPP exposure are agonists. Though, the compounds have different target enzymes. Compound 4550 targets enzyme 26002 (MOXD1), compound 4635 targets enzyme 6817 (SULT1A1), compound 6314 targets enzyme 4128 (MAOA) and compound 6618 targets enzyme 124907837 (no HGNC symbol).

# Save results

```{r}
# Export results for collaborative analysis
saveRDS(significant_hits, "hit_targets.rds")
```
